#4275. A.O.T 3 Final Preview: Possibly Shaping Up To Be One of the Best Anime Adaptation Video Games

This is DualShockers' preview of Attack on Titan 3, the penultimate entry in the AOT Video Game series developed by Omega Force and published by Koei Tecmo.

The Attack on Titan series by Hajime Isayama is genuinely one of the most important works for fans worldwide. The show has sparked a massive debate over its controversial ending, but putting that aside, you can’t argue with its overall impact: brilliant storytelling and action that fans will remember for ages.

DualShockers played A.O.T. 3 at a preview event, slashing Titans and humans alike, with the entirety of Attack on Titan's story being adapted.

And now, eight years after the last game in the franchise, Koei Tecmo’s Omega Force is back with Attack on Titan 3. The full game launches next month in December on the PS5, Xbox Series X and S, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2. At DualShockers, we had the opportunity to check out a final preview build, and I must say, as a veteran fan of both the series and the games, they’re truly going out swinging on this one.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling. You see, back then there was this evident problem that Omega Force could only adapt parts of the story since the anime was still airing, which meant that you weren’t going to get the full package, or at least, where the manga had reached in contrast to the show.

With AOT3, it still remains true to the storytelling presentation of the prior entries. But rather than simply allowing you to relive the anime's biggest moments through the familiar cast, this game once again introduces an original character for you to create and customize.

Our OC character suffers a devastating loss after their previous squad is wiped out during a Titan encounter beyond the walls. So, after developing a fear of Titans from the incident, they're removed from active duty and assigned to instruct the 104th Cadet Corps. This gives you a chance to interact with familiar faces such as Eren, Armin, and Mikasa before eventually graduating from the instructor role and taking command of your own reconnaissance squad.

This approach is very promising because it gives Omega Force a chance to explore parts of the Attack on Titan universe that don't necessarily receive the same attention in the anime. You're not another member of Eren's generation experiencing everything alongside him. But instead, you're an experienced soldier watching these young cadets grow into the people who will eventually shape humanity's fate.

There are also original story events and character interactions designed to expand on the relationships between your character and the existing cast, which is a very nice gesture for us longtime fans if we want something new from this whole experience, especially for characters that didn’t get a ton of screen time in the main show or earlier seasons.

DualShockers spoke to A.O.T. 3 producer Hideo Suzuki about the new Titans, balancing grittiness with arcade action, and why there's no romance.

Of course, none of this hard work over the past 8 years would matter nearly as much without the one thing that makes AOT such an exciting property to adapt into a video game: its combat.

Fortunately, Omega Force hasn't simply brought back the same Omni-Directional Mobility (ODM) system from Attack on Titan 2 and called it a day. The studio has made several adjustments to how you can move around the battlefield, giving the familiar grappling mechanics far more flexibility while also adding new layers of strategy to Titan encounters.

Previously, much of the combat revolved around attaching your ODM anchors to a Titan, reeling yourself towards it, and timing your attack to strike its nape. While that foundation remains intact, AOT3 has generally put more emphasis on identifying weaknesses before committing to an attack. The gameplay rhythm now feels more like a hybrid between a strategic action game.

You can now target individual body parts, allowing you to damage limbs, interrupt attacks, and temporarily immobilize Titans before going for the finishing blow. This is especially important because these guys are much more aggressive, with new attack patterns that require you to watch their movements rather than blindly rush toward their weak spots.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling.

Other noticeably uplifting additions include the maneuverability upgrades and defensive options. You can attach yourself to certain surfaces to reposition, use boost jumps to gain additional height, and even dive or slide along the ground to avoid incoming attacks, which is very useful when dealing with larger Titans during their one-on-one boss fight encounters where you have to stun them for the one-hit kill from their nape area.

As for defensive mechanics, you can use well-timed dodges and parries to defend against incoming attacks. Combat Arts also add another layer of progression, giving you access to powerful unlockable special attacks as you increase your military rank. It's an ambitious evolution of the combat from the prior entries, one that I’m very excited to experience to a greater extent with the full release.

The overall game’s flow looks extremely ambitious, and what I mean is that the game has three working gears in motion for the full package here: interacting with your squadmates at the base, the main story missions that progress the campaign, and your Exterior missions.

The latter is one of the highlights, as it lets you freely explore the world with your squad in tow to hunt down more Titans and fulfil different requests from NPCs you come across. It’s essentially a way to give you more gameplay freedom instead of railroading you from start to finish to showcase the anime's main story, and doing Exterior missions also lets you reap additional rewards and useful upgrade materials, which you definitely need and can’t skip since they let you enhance your equipment.

And speaking of gameplay freedom, you can put any doubts to rest about whether you can jump into this game without prior experience with how the first two games worked. There are a bunch of accessibility and control scheme options that let any player easily enjoy the story, but if you want total control, you can turn off any options that automate the combat mechanics, which I honestly prefer since you’re way more vulnerable to mistakes that way, and it makes the game more punishing.

Still, I can promise you that Attack on Titan 3 is genuinely worth having on your radar for the December releases. With how much I got to sample here, I can’t wait to see how more of the character interactions play out, how the talent points fully work with everything in place, along with how the noteworthy battles in the show play out here, and that includes the whole sections of Marley from Season 4 and beyond. It is a lot to look forward to on my side, but I’ll gladly march into battle head-on with my goth Scout Corps Captain.

#4273. A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math

For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies

To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important.

The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children

An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes."

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4272. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4270. Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an important step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging

When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

However, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

"That put me on a different path," said Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work."

Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

New DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work

Sehgal is the lead author of the new study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

"For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," said Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions."

Biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

These tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

Across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

"What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal said. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers."

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

One of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating plan consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.)

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another important finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months."

That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

"We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he said. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood."

Important Questions About Slowing Aging Remain

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how quickly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures showed little measurable effect.

These results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

Materials provided by Yale University. Original written by Karen Guzman. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

So the full game is now titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel, or, as we will undoubtedly refer to it moving forward, as we colloquially do with the previous three games (Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim), Sentinel.

The news comes from Bethesda's various social media accounts, which are all sharing the video above. Along with the video, music, and the title, it also shares the text as a quote attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest to High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell (4E 206): "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. Sentinel is one of the nine major kingdoms within Hammerfell and is the capital of both the Alik'r Desert region and the Myrkwasa region of the Alik'r (source: elderscrolls.fandom). With this knowledge, it's fair to assume Sentinel will have many desert locations.

The name continues the tradition of naming the games after locations in the Elder Scrolls universe. Oblivion is the sort of exception, as it is a realm, but it still counts. We still don't know exactly when The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel will be released, but we're now about seven years from its original announcement at E3 2018.

#4265. Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.

#4264. Inside is a moody, critically acclaimed little indie platformer, coming to Android

With all the big, flashy games releasing on mobile lately, you may have missed a humble but critically acclaimed game set to launch on Android. Yes, Playdead's seminal indie platformer Inside is coming to Android, with pre-registration now open so you can find out exactly what all the fuss has been about.

In Inside, you play as a young boy in a world of technological horror, evading various hazards in your quest to find out what exactly is going on. Like Playdead's most famous game, Limbo, it's a moody, monochrome platformer that has you exploring a winding world of surreal and frightening imagery.

I think that helps to sell Inside to people too, as many indie platformers get slapped with the label of walking simulator. But while Inside has plenty of those elements with its experimental graphics, linear progression and strange, esoteric story, it's got plenty of challenge that means you can't simply press right and keep going.

Inside is also available on iOS, and has been planned for Android for a while. But now, it seems we won't need to wait long to get our hands on what is arguably Playdead's defining release.

#4262. 10 Best Soulslikes With Fluid Movement Mechanics

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Soulslikes represent a subgenre of ARPGs with quite distinct characteristics, including various constraints intended to establish their aggressive and challenging nature.

Features such as combat that prioritize functionality over spectacle, as well as limited and mundane traversal methods, are a constant among Soulsborne games' descendants, precisely because they exploit these limitations to create immersive experiences.

It's an incredibly delicate balance because, if poorly executed, it leads to clunky campaigns where the mere act of moving from one place to another can become tedious, though there are also exceptions that prove the rule.

Therefore, in order to shed light on these anomalies and draw on the contributions of titles with a lighter approach to the genre, here are the ten best Soulslikes with fluid movement mechanics.

Since I first played it, I think I've been one of Elden Ring Nightreign's most fervent critics, as it's a title that constantly contradicts me to the point of including it in a list of Soulslikes despite being developed by FromSoftware.

However, if there's one thing I not only can't complain about, but which I sincerely find masterful within the genre, it's the way it agilizes movement to a maximum. It gives each playthrough a dynamism uncommon in the genre.

Thanks to the characters' speed, their ability to climb walls, the spirit streams to jump to incredible heights, and the Spectral Hawk flight, which allows you to hover over areas with remarkable accuracy regarding your landing spot, simply wandering around is quite satisfying—a statement I can't make about almost any other title of this kind.

Is it cheating to include a game from the original influences' roots, which is also more of a roguelite, in this list? Perhaps, yet this is the first time the study has taken movement so seriously, so it deserves the mention.

Phantom Blade Zero is a fusion of traditional action-adventure elements with ideas borrowed from both Soulslikes and Metroidvanias, creating an extravagant yet highly satisfying cocktail.

The game boasts a staggering array of flashy weapons whose visual grandeur is breathtaking, especially in the hands of an ultra-powerful protagonist who is capable of putting those tools at the movement's mercy.

With the ability to sprint at high speed, swing on chains to cross gaps, run along walls, and use a grappling hook to reach high points, this title refuses to simply block doors on one side but instead strives to add depth to the exploration.

Unfortunately, most of these mechanics are prompts that can only be activated at specific, controlled locations, but they are more than enough to make Phantom Blade Zero a more dynamic game than average in this regard.

If you’re looking for the best FromSoftware-inspired ARPGs, I recommend the best Soulslikes based on critics' scores.

Speaking of middle ground, Nine Sols takes Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice's combat system and Hollow Knight's perspective, platforming, and exploration to create one of the decade's most wonderful indie games.

While it leans towards one or the other inspiration depending on the context, it's incredible how Yi soars across the maps once you've unlocked all of his movement tools, which are simple in concept but incredibly rewarding in execution.

Surely, it's nothing more than double jumps, dashes, and kicking enemies' skulls to get airborne, but it's enough to perfectly complement his prodigious combat mechanics.

Even if Nine Sols had terrible traversal, it would still be great because of how it shines in all the other elements, making the polished movement mechanics all the more admirable.

Especially considering it was released when Soulslikes were still in their infancy, Salt and Sanctuary was a major surprise, perfectly adapting the genre's formula to the 2D side-scrolling perspective.

With a wealth of secrets hidden behind the movement abilities you progressively unlock, it's a title that knows how to make platforming satisfying and imbue it with meaning beyond simply moving from point A to point B.

When you first change the gravity orientation, for example, you realize Salt and Sanctuary isn't just a great action RPG with challenging bosses and outstanding worldbuilding, but a game that understood that part of the Dark Souls trilogy's charm lay in how it transformed each new tool into a way to reinterpret the levels.

Years have passed, and I still believe it's the purest and most outstanding 2D Soulslike among those that don't venture too far into other genres, as few have captured the essence of their inspiration as well as this one.

Team Ninja is among the developers that have placed the most emphasis on the Soulslike genre, and while Rise of the Ronin isn't their most outstanding iteration, it certainly stands out when movement is the key factor.

Based on its open-world concept, the game boasts one of the most inventive arrays of traversal tools the genre has ever seen, offering a horse, a grappling hook, and a glider to facilitate the discovery of its expansive map.

If you compare it to direct peers like Ghost of Tsushima, it might fall short, but if the conversation turns to previous titles from the studio, such as Nioh, or games from FromSoftware, like the aforementioned Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, the tone shifts.

Ultimately, Rise of the Ronin combines a myriad of ideas that will appeal to some and deter others, though the fact that it brings with it a form of exploration that avoids relying solely on walking and fast travel is undeniable.

If you’re still waiting for the next FromSoftware game, check out these ten Soulslikes that most people haven’t played but definitely should.

Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King is a fascinating title due to its attempt, although often erratic, to combine 3D combat with side-scrolling platforming, which is a unique approach even outside Soulslikes' spaces.

The combat is present and functional enough to sustain the experience for the hours it lasts, yet what truly catches the eye is the movement, as it feels like Journey thanks to its flow and smoothness.

In addition to its perspective shifts, which alternate between combat and 2.5D traversal, moving through its open world on a hoverboard feels compelling, mainly because of how unexpected it is to encounter such a mechanic in this type of game.

Indeed, there isn't much to do once you're in free-roaming areas, but since this article focuses on movement mechanics, Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King keeps its place among the most distinguished in the genre.

While the first game in the series was pure action-adventure, and the second shifted towards open-world RPG elements, Darksiders 3 changed course once again, this time aiming to be both a Soulslike and a Metroidvania.

By merging the level design and combat system of the former with the progression and backtracking mechanics of the latter, Gunfire Games created a phenomenal symphony that truly draws on its hack-and-slash heritage.

Darksiders 3 embraces grandeur, allowing you to transform into diverse avatars to double jump and burn through barriers, glide on air currents, become an energy ball to cling to walls, or even walk on water.

If you add to all these different ways of traversing the use of Fury's whip to swing from platform to platform, the only logical conclusion left to draw is that Darksiders 3 is a marvel when it comes to moving around.

Another Crab's Treasure is among the most creatively designed Soulslikes we've had the pleasure of enjoying this decade, and its movement mechanics are anything but an exception.

The game's levels are extremely vertical and branching, so it needed movement methods that could handle its demanding platforming sections with jumps, climbs, glides, and directional grappling hooks that take you from one ledge to another in a matter of seconds.

It's no wonder the game has become a favorite among speedrunners; its open areas combined with its fluid maneuverability create the perfect breeding ground for exploring the limits of gravity and Krill's stamina.

It has incredible bosses, extensive customization, a remarkable audiovisual component, strong thematic cohesion... Another Crab's Treasure is a complete package, and thankfully, Aggro Crab didn't leave platforming out of the equation.

If you're looking for community-endorsed experiences, I recommend you try these ten Soulslikes where the user score is higher than the critic score.

After Hollow Knight established the Soulslite variant as an alternative for those who didn't want to fully commit to the formula, Hollow Knight: Silksong further solidified its fresh take on the genre.

The loss of resources upon death, save points that also serve as locations to modify your character, pattern-based bosses, cryptic lore... We all know the points of convergence, but where it truly breaks away is in its movement.

Even when compared to pure platformers, Hollow Knight: Silksong possesses a unique grace when it comes to traversal, with an incredibly agile Hornet who's capable of using her abilities in unique ways to facilitate her journey through Pharloom.

Grabbing ledges, bouncing off environmental elements, flying on air currents, leaping between walls, using your needle to propel yourself forward... The array of abilities available during the game is incredible and, above all, very satisfying, especially when you learn to chain them together and run without anything or anyone stopping you.

Nevertheless, beyond the games made by FromSoftware itself or titles that only tangentially touch on the genre, the purest example of a Soulslike with the most fluid movement mechanics is Valor Mortis.

Coming from Ghostrunner, One More Level leveraged its undeniable aptitude for first-person platforming and created an entire world around it, giving us an adventure where you jump, dash, swoop, and grapple with impressive ease.

Valor Mortis is already a striking project for its combination of such divergent concepts as stealth, first-person shooting, and ARPG combat based on parries, though adding such natural platforming sections on top of all that is simply incredible.

I spent the entire campaign amazed by the simple fact that Soulslikes don't move this fast and seamlessly, much less in sequences where you're speeding around in a minecart or running across platforms that are collapsing because a giant monster is attacking you with its tentacles.

Valor Mortis is a game that can be criticized for many things, but not for its movement. In fact, this is an area where it excels so much that other games should strive to emulate its talent.

From the indie ecosystem to productions approaching AAA measures, these are ten Soulslike franchises that should come back by 2027.

With the holiday gift-giving season upon us, it’s time to think about the gaming fans in your life and find the ideal present to brighten their day. #4259. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4257. Jordan Esports Federation signs MoU with King Hussein Business Park to host more events

Priya Venkatesh has been following the money in esports since before brand deals were considered legitimate marketing. She got pulled into the scene through competitive fighting games and eventually found herself more interested in the contracts and partnerships behind the tournaments than the matches themselves. These days she focuses on how brands navigate esports sponsorships, where the smart money is going, and which deals are actually built to last versus the ones that look good in a press release.

The Jordan Esports Federation (JEF) has signed a memorandum of understanding with King Hussein Business Park (KHBP) in Amman, giving the national body a formal framework to stage more tournaments and events at the site it already calls home.

KHBP announced the deal on Sunday in a statement published on its website. Prince Omar bin Faisal, who is President of the JEF, attended the signing.

Under the MoU, the federation and the business park will jointly host and organise specialised competitions on the KHBP campus. They will also receive the international delegations and official guests that travel to those events. Beyond the competitive side, the two organisations plan to cooperate on media and marketing, look at shared education, training and community projects, and swap knowledge and expertise.

Neither party has disclosed financial terms or the length of the agreement.

KHBP CEO Eng. Ammar Ezzeddin presented the MoU as part of the park’s wider ambitions. “This partnership builds on our ongoing efforts to create an enabling environment for institutions, initiatives and high-potential sectors, and to establish KHBP as a hub for innovation and technology,” he said.

He added: “We look forward to helping the sector thrive and to hosting more tournaments and events that put Jordanian talent in the spotlight and raise the Kingdom’s profile in this field.”

JEF Vice President Hazem Bawab focused on the competitive and grassroots goals. “This partnership is a significant step in our drive to develop the esports industry in Jordan and elevate the standard of local, regional and international competitions and activities,” he said.

Bawab continued: “We look forward to drawing on the setup and capabilities that KHBP offers to scale our work, nurture young talent and launch joint programmes that help the industry grow and encourage greater participation.”

The deal formalises a relationship that already exists on the ground. According to The Esports Radar, the JEF, which is the government recognised regulator for esports in the country, is based at the park in West Amman.

A lot of that work happens at THE ARC, the arena and gaming dome inside the park. The same report lists past events there including the fourth Arab Esports League, a Women’s Esports Championship and Red Bull Login, which doubled as Jordan’s national final stage in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2. The venue is also an incubation centre supported by the federation and the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship, and runs training camps for players hoping to turn professional.

KHBP has been a destination for esports investment for some time. In 2024, lounge operator True Gamers announced plans for an esports venue in Jordan at the business park, a project in which its CPO publicly thanked the JEF and Prince Omar.

The timing also puts Amman in the industry spotlight. PocketGamer.biz points out that Pocket Gamer Connects Jordan takes place on 7 and 8 November, bringing many of the region’s games industry stakeholders to the city later this week.

It’s a cute game that will, I’m sure, appeal to fans of the genre. But they lost me at the hard-to-get fish. Sorry.

Momolitos is a creature collector with simple animated cartoon graphics. You are situated in the MOMOlab, where you can teleport to an area to collect food and eggs. Back at the lab, you hatch the eggs and feed food to the creatures to make them evolve. The game opens up as you earn orbs.

#4253. KRÜ Blaze win Game Changers Championship from lower bracket, ending Gentle Mates’ unbeaten run

KRÜ Blaze came through the lower bracket to beat Europe's Gentle Mates GC over five maps in São Paulo, giving LATAM its first Game Changers Championship title. They are also the last winners of the standalone event, as next year's final moves to Champions.

KRÜ Blaze are the 2026 VALORANT Game Changers Championship winners. They edged Gentle Mates GC 3-2 at the Riot Games Arena in São Paulo on 1 November. No Latin American team had lifted the title before. No team had ever won it from the lower bracket either.

The event ran from 22 October, with 10 teams competing. Gentle Mates earned US$100,000 as runners-up. Shopify Rebellion Gold took US$70,000 for third place and MIBR GC US$50,000 for fourth.

KRÜ took the long route. They beat Gen.G GC 2-1 in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 23 October. A 2-0 loss to Shopify Rebellion Gold on 27 October then dropped them into the lower bracket. They answered with clean sweeps of Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. On 31 October they beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 3-1 in the best-of-five lower-bracket final.

The grand final swung back and forth. Gentle Mates took Haven 13-5 before KRÜ levelled on Abyss by the same score. KRÜ led the third map 10-2 at half-time. Gentle Mates fought back, but KRÜ closed it out 14-12 in overtime. Gentle Mates then won Split 13-8 to force a decider. KRÜ led 11-5 on Ascent and won it by the same margin as Split.

Liquipedia named KRÜ’s Argentine player tok1o as the event’s MVP. Brazilian teammates antG and none became the first Brazilians to win an international tournament held in São Paulo.

The result breaks a pattern. Before 2026 the title went to G2 Gozen for Europe in 2022, Shopify Rebellion for North America in 2023 and 2024, and Team Liquid Brazil in 2025. KRÜ’s own record at the event had improved steadily. They finished 7th–8th in 2022 and 5th–6th in each of the next two years. Last year they came fourth.

For European fans, it was a painful near miss. Gentle Mates GC arrived as EMEA’s top seed on circuit points. The team had not lost a series in São Paulo before the final, according to Esports News UK.

It capped a strong debut season in the circuit. Gentle Mates won EMEA Stage 1 by sweeping G2 Gozen 3-0 on 22 February. They lost the Stage 2 final to SK Nebula on 24 May without winning a map. On 30 August they lost the Stage 3 final to G2 Gozen in a fifth map. Silver in São Paulo leaves them with one title from four finals this year.

After a lower bracket run in São Paulo, the LATAM squad claimed the #VCTGameChangers Championship trophy! pic.twitter.com/YeSeb10TZc

— VCT Pacific (@vctpacific) November 1, 2026

The São Paulo final also closes a format. KRÜ are the last team to lift the trophy at a separate event of its own. For the first time, the Game Changers Championship will finish at Champions. Under Riot’s 2027 plan, non-partner teams that qualify for the Game Changers Championship will receive an extra US0,000 incentive. VALORANT Champions 2027 is scheduled for 16 September to 10 October in Austin.

#4252. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

#4251. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4245. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4244. PlayStation Adds Major Feature to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, ARC Raiders, and More

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

A big component of what makes the PS5 an attractive console, besides just being able to play particular games you can’t play elsewhere, is the console’s various built-in graphical perks. Since the PS5 first launched in 2020, its hardware power has remained one of its definitive perks, with the PS5 Pro in particular taking matters further with the inclusion of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, better known as PSSR.

In this list, we discuss some of the best PS4 games to play with the PS5 Pro's Image Quality Enhancements option.

Even though the PS5 already has a few years under its belt, the brand isn’t just resting on its proverbial laurels and letting its existing hardware carry it. New advancements in graphical technology are coming out all the time, and even games that looked pretty stunning when they first dropped like Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 can always look a little bit better.

To that end, PlayStation has added support for one of its up-and-coming graphical frameworks, Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), to several more games in the PS5’s library following its initial launch last month exclusively in Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei. The newly-upscaled games include Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, Control Resonant, ARC Raiders, The Finals, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam.

In case you forgot, QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD. This framework came about from Project Amethyst, an ongoing developmental effort between both companies that also gave rise to PSSR. According to the official announcement of the newly-upscaled games on the official PlayStation news blog, QSSR provides “sharper details, cleaner edges, and more stable images than traditional upscalers,” and since it’s built on the same platform as PSSR, it’s easy for games that already use that framework to incorporate it.

QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD.

In that news post, PlayStation got quotes from all of the improved games’ developers on how QSSR has affected their respective titles. Insomniac Games’ Mike Fitzgerald said that, after incorporating the tech into the launch of Marvel’s Wolverine, the studio decided to go back and add it to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 as well. “We’re excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see QSSR’s exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both Fidelity and Performance modes,” he said.

Sony has introduced a brand-new AI-powered upscaling technology called Quick Spectral Super Resolution.

Remedy Entertainment’s Erik Jansson said that “QSSR gives Control Resonant a much more stable and detailed image, and we’ve worked closely with Sony to have it ready in an update coming in December.”

Embark Studios’ Mikael Linderholm said that QSSR support will be coming soon to ARC Raiders and The Finals, and said that his studio is “very happy to see Sony’s continued investment in PlayStation technology translate into meaningful improvements for all players.”

While I’m personally of the belief that graphics alone don’t automatically make a game good, it is still pretty interesting to see the degree to which graphical fidelity can be improved, especially as we start to run up against the proverbial limits of realism.

Obviously, the use of AI in games is a feisty topic, particularly in presentation elements like voice acting. In the specific use case of graphics, some efforts like NVIDIA’s AI-powered DLSS5 and its widely-mocked “yassify filter” on character models is probably not the optimal way to be going about this. Rather than trying to generate and overwrite existing graphics with slop, something like QSSR is closer to the ideal, taking what’s already present and merely smoothing out the rougher edges of the environmental rendering process.

PlayStation has promised that this tech will be coming to more games, ending its news post by saying, “Developers are just getting started, and we’re excited to keep working with them to bring QSSR to more games on PS5 in the coming months.”

Two classic apocalyptic shooters have received free modern graphical facelifts.
