#4213. Ocarina of Time Remake Finally Gives Zelda’s Saddest Story the Attention It Deserves

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

After nearly 30 years, the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is finally here, and it's already winning over critics and fans alike – myself included. As I highlighted in my review, this new version embodies what a modern remake should be: an experience that embraces contemporary improvements without losing the old soul of the classic we all love!

And one of the things I've always loved about Ocarina of Time is how many curious characters are scattered throughout Hyrule. Some have surprisingly elaborate backstories, while others barely give you enough information to understand what's going on. More often than not, you need to be genuinely curious to piece together their stories and figure out what they're doing in the world.

My favorite example, by far, is Grog, a rather strange-looking punk who barely appeared in the original game but arguably had one of its saddest stories. Much of what made his character so fascinating came from the lovely fan theories surrounding his family and his mysterious disappearance.

To my surprise, the Switch 2 remake doesn't just subtly address some of those theories, but it also expands Grog's story in ways that make his already tragic arc considerably more meaningful. And to appreciate just how much has changed, we first need to revisit what made this little side story so memorable in the first place.

First things first, let's remember how Grog's story unfolded in the original Ocarina of Time. The character only appeared in two locations throughout the entire adventure: beneath a tree in Kakariko Village at night as Child Link, and later in the Lost Woods as Adult Link.

In Kakariko Village, you'll find him sitting beneath the tree in the center of town, looking rather miserable. Talk to him, and you'll quickly discover that he's not exactly the friendliest person around. He's withdrawn, bitter, and apparently hates just about everyone – including Link, simply for daring to approach him! And that's pretty much all you get from this first encounter.

To my surprise, the Switch 2 remake doesn't just subtly address some of those theories, but it also expands Grog's story in ways that make his already tragic arc considerably more meaningful.

His second appearance, however, is where things get interesting. As Adult Link, you can find Grog in the Lost Woods, but getting him to appear requires a little detour. First, you need to talk to the Cucco Lady in Kakariko Village, who turns out to be Grog's sister. She explains that he had a falling-out with their father, the village's Master Craftsman, and eventually left home. She's worried about him, though, so she gives you an egg that eventually hatches into Cojiro, Grog's beloved blue Cucco.

After using Cojiro to wake up Talon in Kakariko Village, you can take the Cucco into the Lost Woods. That's when you'll finally find Grog again, now seven years later, sitting in a rather strange, almost lifeless state. However, showing him Cojiro seems to snap him out of it, and he asks you to take an Odd Mushroom to the Granny's Potion Shop so she can prepare a medicine for him.

There's just one problem: when you return with the medicine, Grog is nowhere to be found. Instead, you're greeted by Fado, one of the Kokiri children, who explains that he disappeared into the Lost Woods. She also tells you that adults who get lost in the forest turn into Stalfos – those skeletal enemies that have been giving Link a hard time throughout the adventure.

And just like that, Grog's story appears to come to an end. The implication is pretty heartbreaking: the troubled young man who left home after a disagreement with his father has seemingly lost himself in the forest, never to return.

But even that brief story leaves plenty of unanswered questions. What exactly happened between Grog and his father? Why was he so unhappy? And what was the medicine supposed to cure? The original game never gave us definitive answers, leaving players to connect the dots through scattered dialogue and a handful of subtle clues. Thankfully, the remake finally gives us a much closer look at what was going on!

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

One of the most interesting additions in the remake is a new time system that allows the day-night cycle to progress naturally even while you're exploring towns and villages. Outside of more contained areas, such as dungeons and minigame shops, NPCs now follow their own schedules, appearing in different locations and going about their daily routines.

It's a relatively small change, but it makes Hyrule feel considerably more alive – and if you're a fan of Majora's Mask, you'll probably appreciate the familiar feeling of watching characters follow their own little agendas instead of simply standing around waiting for Link to show up!

Outside of more contained areas, such as dungeons and minigame shops, NPCs now follow their own schedules, appearing in different locations and going about their daily routines.

More importantly, this new system gives us additional opportunities to learn about Grog when playing as Child Link. For starters, you can now find him during the day near the entrance to Kakariko Village's graveyard. He's officially identified as the Master Craftsman's Son, making his connection to the village's grumpy carpenter much clearer from the beginning. Talk to him (or simply get close enough to hear him mumbling to himself) and you'll discover that his hatred for practically everything is closely tied to his strained relationship with his father.

And speaking of the Master Craftsman, the remake also gives us a better look at his daily routine. He and his assistants no longer spend all their time repeating the same actions in the same spots. Instead, they're spread throughout the village, and they even gather in front of the central tree for a meeting as the day comes to an end.

Talking to the assistants reveals that they also find their boss rather difficult to deal with. He's a grumpy, demanding man who seems to have a complaint about just about everything. Yet, interestingly enough, none of those complaints ever seem to involve Grog. While his son is clearly consumed by their strained relationship, the Master Craftsman barely acknowledges that anything is wrong – or just wants to ignore it.

But my favorite addition is that you can actually follow Grog around Kakariko Village throughout the day. He eventually gets up from his spot and sneaks behind a pile of bricks near the construction site overseen by his father. There, he quietly mutters that he needs to wait for the Master Craftsman to leave before he can go inside.

And when night finally falls, Grog makes his way back to the central tree, recreating the exact scene we remember from the original game. It's such a small sequence, but it adds an entirely new layer to his character. We no longer just see a miserable young man sitting beneath a tree. We see someone who is actively avoiding his father, seemingly unable to find a way to repair their relationship. And considering what we eventually learn about Grog, that little detail becomes even more heartbreaking.

The remake also expands Grog's story when playing as Adult Link, particularly through additional dialogue with his sister and mother. As in the original, you'll only encounter Grog in the Lost Woods once you reach the point in the Biggoron Sword side quest where Cojiro has turned blue. However, the Cucco Lady now has considerably more information to share about why her brother left home in the first place.

According to her, Grog didn't want to follow the family business. While their father expected him to become a carpenter, Grog wanted to work with animals, something he was particularly passionate about and apparently quite good at. The Master Craftsman strongly disapproved of this decision, and their disagreement eventually caused a complete breakdown in their relationship.

This is a pretty significant addition because it finally gives us a clearer picture of what happened between the two. Grog wasn't simply a rebellious young man who decided to leave home. He had his own dreams and interests, but his father couldn't accept that his son wanted a different future.

After hearing this, you can head into the Lost Woods and follow the original sequence. Grog is still there, seemingly trapped in the same strange state, and showing him Cojiro produces the same reaction as before. He snaps out of it and asks you to take the Odd Mushroom to the Granny's Potion Shop.

However, Granny also has a few new things to say! She confirms that Grog has been acting foolishly by distancing himself from his family, adding another perspective to the conflict. It's a small exchange, but it helps establish that this isn't just a disagreement between a father and son. So yes, the entire family has been affected by Grog's departure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has finally been released, and fans have already discovered several game-breaking glitches.

Unfortunately, things take the same tragic turn when you return to the Lost Woods with the medicine. Grog is gone, and Fado is waiting in his place. This time, however, the encounter is considerably more unsettling. She immediately notices the medicine's smell and desperately asks you to hand it over, offering a tool Grog left behind in exchange. Then, she explains that adults who enter the forest and lose their way, just like Grog apparently did, eventually turn into Stalfos.

But the story doesn't quite end there. You can return to Kakariko Village and talk to the Cucco Lady again, who provides even more information about her brother. She explains that she now takes care of the Cuccos because Grog left home after refusing to become a carpenter. In other words, her own life has also been shaped by the same family conflict that drove him away. And she’s also still hopeful that her brother is okay and will be back someday.

Finally, you can take the tool Grog left behind to the Master Craftsman, who is now waiting near the entrance to Gerudo Valley. He recognizes it as something he had given his son and explains that he had asked Grog to return it personally. Instead, his son apparently chose to send someone else to do the job.

It's a rather dismissive reaction, especially considering everything we've learned about their relationship. Even after Grog has disappeared, his father seems more concerned about the way he returned a tool than the fact that he may never see his son again.

What always fascinated me about Grog's story in the original Ocarina of Time was how much the game managed to communicate without ever explicitly explaining anything. It gave us scattered clues, brief conversations, and seemingly unrelated characters who slowly revealed their connections to one another. The rest was left to the players, who spent years discussing theories about Grog, his family, and what might have happened to him.

The remake takes those little pieces and finally puts them together. We now know exactly why Grog left home, what caused the rift with his father, and how his decision affected the rest of his family. And while the game still leaves some things open to interpretation, his story feels much more complete.

What I particularly love about this addition is that it doesn't try to turn Grog into some incredibly important character or give him an elaborate questline that changes the entire adventure. Instead, it simply gives more attention to a person who was already part of Hyrule, allowing us to understand the struggles that were always hiding behind his grumpy attitude.

And there's something genuinely sad about realizing that the Stalfos we encounter throughout the game might have once been people with their own dreams, families, and reasons for entering the forest. Grog's story makes that possibility feel much more personal. After all, he wasn't some nameless traveler who got lost. He was a young man who wanted to follow his own path, but never managed to find a way back home.

We now know exactly why Grog left home, what caused the rift with his father, and how his decision affected the rest of his family. And while the game still leaves some things open to interpretation, his story feels much more complete.

I also love how this expanded story fits into what makes Ocarina of Time so special! Hyrule isn't just a collection of locations for Link to explore, but a world filled with people whose lives continue beyond the moments when we interact with them. Sometimes, all it takes is a few extra lines of dialogue or a character walking to a different spot at sunset to make that world feel considerably richer.

Of course, I still have one personal theory I'd rather believe. Maybe Grog didn't actually turn into a Stalfos. Maybe he discovered the secret entrance to Termina, found his way to Clock Town, and eventually became the Cucco-loving man we meet in Majora's Mask. After all, if there's anyone who deserves a happy ending surrounded by the animals he loves, it's Grog. And after everything this remake has revealed about his family, I think I'll keep believing that version of the story.

#4212. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.0 brings a new world, and a Fortnite collaboration

Honkai: Star Rail's next major update introduces a whole new planet to the RPG, and way more besides.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

The upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big new world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

As you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

If you log in after launch, you’ll get 20 free pulls and a new free outfit for Ruan Mei. If you play while the Yao Guang fortune event is active, you could earn 1,600 Stellar Jades. You can also expect a free 5-Star character selector to arrive at some point after launch, giving you a free choice between popular (but admittedly a bit old for the meta these days) limited-banner characters Jing Yuan, Kafka, Dan Heng • Imbibitor Lunae, Jingliu, Sparkle, Acheron, and Aventurine.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

#4210. Award-Winning Composer And Musician Jon Batiste Talks Ocarina Of Time's Music And Why 'Guile's Theme' Goes With Everything

Jon Batiste has collaborated with the likes of Alicia Keys, Lenny Kravitz, Prince, Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, and many more. He performed the national anthem at Super Bowl LIX. He's headed up the musical efforts of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He's taken home more awards than we can realistically list in this article (including eight Grammys, as well as an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe). But as I sit down with Batiste for a brief conversation about video game music, his energy transcends the Zoom call.

Before I can even ask a question, Batiste begins singing to greet me, then nerds out about my NBA Jam and Street Fighter II cabinets. He begins humming the menu music from NBA Jam and reminiscing about all the quarters he pumped into his local Street Fighter cabinet. The Louisiana native and Juilliard School alum has been an ardent gaming enthusiast for nearly three decades, with compositions from games like Sonic the Hedgehog and Final Fantasy VII inspiring his earliest musical endeavors. Spend enough time watching video game music performances on social media, and you'll likely soon find videos of Batiste sitting with famed Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu, or of Batiste performing gaming music.

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to New York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

Ocarina of Time is easily one of the most important video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power! So, you could listen to the music in the game, and you could also listen to it apart from the game and experience that magic.

Are there any tracks in Ocarina of Time that stand out to you as the most musically sophisticated or compositionally impressive?Oh man. Well, I think of it as a suite, so that's what makes it actually... there's nothing that's more or less complex, but the thought to figure out how to make all of the themes be interrelated yet singular. "Song of Storms" is, like, for me, that's a personal favorite. That's why I like to play it. I like to play a lot of the themes. That's how I grew up! I would play the game, and then, I would go to an instrument. Once we played for hours on Nintendo, we'd go and play Nintendo on piano! It was like a trade-off there, you know? I've been doing this since I was about 11 years old.

Taking it back to that 11-year-old Jon, talk to me a little bit about your history in general.Okay, so my history with Nintendo goes back to the NES. Christmas morning. Duck Hunt. You remember that? Maybe the first game I ever played. No, the first game I ever played was Donkey Kong, and then Duck Hunt, and then Super Mario Bros. Staples! We're talking about the early '90s. We had a room where I would go – it was my domain – and we had this blue shag carpet, and I would sit back there, and I would basically disappear into the carpet playing Nintendo for hours and hours.

And my mind is kind of... my mind can become a spiral; it can become a tornado. And I realized even then that going into this world of the game, even if I didn't win – it's not about winning or losing – it helps to organize the spiral of my mind and give me ideas and inspiration. So then, I started to get into Street Fighter II when I started to play more communally with my sister and my cousins. Yoko Shimomura, who I also had the pleasure of meeting and collaborating with, she composed incredible themes for each character, and that's when I really started to get a true love for fighting games.

And then, we would play so many of the Street Fighter franchise. We would play a lot of Final Fight. There were so many things... there was Double Dragon, then we got Mega Man... all these different series. Mega Man X is [an] all-time favorite. And then, here comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and that sort of expands the canon while also blending all of the elements: score, combat, the sort of linear quality of, like, a Donkey Kong or Super Mario World, and expanding the world in that way, expanding the canon in that way. Mind-blowing! So,  that sort of solidified my palate in terms of my favorite type of game.

You mentioned Street Fighter II. There's a meme about "Guile's Theme" and how it goes with everything. What about that composition makes it so it has the ability to enhance whatever video you pair it with?Wow! So, it has momentum in a way that is extremely [sings the melody of "Guile's Theme"] ... It draws you in, which is what you want [with] anything that you're starting when you're commencing a journey or watching something. You want it to draw you in, and that kind of pulls you in as that call and response. But it's an immediate announcement with the brass, and then the bass call and response. So, it's automatically giving you this feeling that something's happening, and I've got to pay attention to it! So that's the first step right there. And the tempo is really... it's a great tempo! It almost has the feeling of the great themes from, like, an '80s protagonist that's in a fighting movie. I think that was kind of the archetype. Yoko was probably drawing from that archetype, right? The action-hero archetype.

#4209. Fable Quest Trailer Ratio’d And Compared To Dragon Age

Xbox has just released a new gameplay trailer for Fable showing one of the game’s quests, but it might not have been the best showcase since it’s being bombarded with dislikes.

Ever since the initial reveal trailer more than six years ago, Fable has easily been one of Xbox’s most highly anticipated games. That excitement has only increased with each gameplay showcase and trailer, which have shown just how far Playground Games has pushed the original trilogy’s mechanics, even if the reboot is leaving some things behind.

Of course, while most people are looking forward to Fable, it’s also been a target for online hate campaigns ever since the second trailer. Recent showings of Fable, including one that was focused on combat, have notably had a lot of backlash, and that drama has all come to a head with the latest trailer for the game.

Earlier this week, the official Fable YouTube account shared a new trailer for the game that highlights a quest where the Hero and Arden investigate what’s happening to Oakshire. The gameplay admittedly isn’t the most exciting thing in the world, since it mostly just shows the Hero walking through the area, getting in a fight, and talking to Arden before a big plot tease at the end.

Fable will let us hit on as many townsfolk as we want, but am I the only one who liked getting at least one proper romance option in Fable 3?

While it’s not a great showcase, the quest trailer is pretty harmless overall in my opinion and not that noteworthy. People don’t seem to agree with that, though, as the trailer is being ratio’d on YouTube with 4,200 dislikes compared to 3,400 likes as of the time of writing and an incredibly negative comments section with some brutal reactions.

One notable trend in the comments section is comparisons to Dragon Age: The Veilguard, with one popular comment calling it “Fable Age: The Veilguard”. Others are simply calling it out as a “disappointing” trailer that ended too soon and didn’t really show anything of substance. As one user puts it, “Is that really the best they can show?”

The Fable account is definitely seeing these negative comments too, as it’s heart-reacted the few positive ones praising the voice acting and graphics.

It’s not just the YouTube video that’s being slammed, either, as Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s post about the trailer on Twitter is also full of backlash and the usual “Sweet Baby Inc” comments over two female characters. Some of it is clearly bad faith, but I’d be very hard-pressed to say the footage was worthy of a trailer.

It's been a long, hard road back to success for Sports Interactive, but FM 27 is the game I hoped it would be and so much more.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4208. Heartopia shows off My Little Pony collaboration, and there's a pre-launch event to hold you over

Heartopia’s My Little Pony collaboration is close, and the pre-launch event has already kicked off.

Heartopia has officially shared initial details about its first-ever collaboration event. The game, which launched a month ago to great success on mobile, as well as Steam on PC, has already been a staple among fans of Animal Crossing and The Sims.

Things are kicking into gear, it seems, because the game is already about to host its first collaboration event, and it is with My Little Pony.

The Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start. The limited-time event offers players sign-in puzzles every day that will unlock time-limited Exhibition Passes.

The first actual piece of My Little Pony-themed content can be yours if you complete all puzzles, as that gets you a limited edition costume for your pet, based on the show’s Spike. The event itself, which will be available until March 15, brings My Little Pony’s Tree of Harmony into the world of Heartopia.

The ponies need your help to Wield Elements of Harmony so they can reawaken the tree, and bring it back to Equestria. In gameplay terms, you’re going to want to perform daily sensing at the tree in order to earn three of the six Elements of Harmony: Honesty, Generosity, Loyalty, Kindness, Laughter, and Magic.

The more you do this, the more the tree’s Energy goes up, and the more rewards and resources you stand to earn. Even more time-limited Exhibition Passes, and Moonlight Crystals can be earned as you water the tree.

Badge Pull Tokens are your big reward, which is what you’re actually going to use to get the special Pony Series badges. You’ll earn ten time-limited Exhibition Passes each time you complete one of the three sets of Pony Series badges. Collect all three and you’ll earn Town Collaboration Series badges.

Heartopia is a free-to-play game, so you know there is a Gacha component to this event. Expect six non-replacement Gacha Pools that each map to one member of My Little Pony’s Mane Six. Within each pool, you’ll be able to earn five outfit pieces, and one vehicle.

If any of that sounds interesting, definitely log in now to play the pre-launch event, which should hold you over until the proper show kicks off Saturday. If you’re already enjoying Heartopia, you likely want to learn about Onsen Egg Promise locations, Fish locations, and Bug locations - all of which can be found at those links.

#4206. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 6, 2026

This week and weekend is all about the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one of the few games I feel deserves the title of masterpiece. And the remake is really well done! I got every heart piece, every Gold Skulltala, the Goron Sword, and the biggest pouch for every one of my items over the course of the review... but I am contemplating jumping right back in for another go.

We also revealed our next cover and in case you missed the announcement it is... pause for effect... Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis! It's an awesome cover that celebrates the history of Lara Croft, and along with a cover story on the game, we also have a big retrospective on the series. I highly recommend subscribing to get your issue if you haven't already.

But it wasn't all just Zelda and Tomb Raider this week. Below you will find a list of weekend play recommendations, but before that... some of our biggest stories of the week.

We have been writing a lot about The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time remake this week because it is one of 2026's most exciting games, and it's real good. The remake is not particularly surprising. It mostly sticks to the trajectory of the original game, but there is a reason it is considered one of the best games of all time. It also looks and plays amazing.

You can read the full review here (or watch the video above), but we also have a big interview with the game's producers (one of whom worked on the original Ocarina of Time, and one who directed Breath of the Wild among many other Zelda games), some details about the Easter Eggs that did and did not make it into the remake, and a very handy tip for the game if you happen to be playing with a Switch 2 Pro controller.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out now and it’s a great time to jump into the revamped and expanded version of a project that changed online games forever back in 2004. A thousand new quests, multiple new zones, countless revamps, and an impressively stunning visual overhaul make it the perfect time to jump in for anyone who’s ever been curious to explore Azeroth.

2022's Escape Academy was a sneaky little puzzle game that surprised me and its sequel released this week. Taking place in a school obsessed with puzzles, you play as a student who must make their way through a series of escape rooms. The puzzles are clever, and the setting is charming, but the secret weapon is the local, split-screen co-op. Solving puzzles together is fun especially when one player needs to look at one section of a room to help dictate a solution on the other side of the room. My wife and I both love video games, but rarely play co-op games together just because of our disparate, individual tastes. But Escape Room is one we enjoyed together and we're so far enjoying the sequel. My only complaint so far is... I wish it ran a little better.

While we collectively use the term here for the sake of familiarity, I’m always a bit hesitant in my own mind to label a game under the wide banner of “Metroidvania.” In part, that’s because I think the two referenced games (Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night) are actually more different than they might appear at first glance. Gloomsoft’s recent release, Moadra, recognizes that distinction, crafting a game that draws heavy inspiration from the specific tradition of Super Metroid, even while presenting an intriguing and atmospheric fiction that is great fun to discover. In movement, actions, and exploration, Moadra feels remarkably similar to  the best of the 2D Metroid games. A scanning tool also leans into the Metroid inspirations, revealing details about the weird alien world you’re navigating. If you’ve been hungry for a game that scratches that particular itch of sci-fi gear/ability-gated exploration, I think you’ll find a lot to love in this game.

I get the Marvel fatigue we've all been experiencing. There are a lot of games and a lot of movies and a lot of TV shows and many are good, but lately most feel like homework. For those reasons, you'd be forgiven for dismissing the 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy game, but I promise you it is good. For one, it is standalone. It does not directly tie to any specific Marvel media. No homework necessary. And for two, it's just a really good game with an affecting story and a unique take on the characters that most of us met for the first time in the movies. And, for the BioWare fans out there mourning the loss of Mass Effect, this game has some Mass Effect energy. It's available on Switch 2 this week and I happily recommend it, especially if you missed it five years ago.

This exclusively two-player board game features a fun mix of activities. You act as both a dungeon architect, and an adventurer delving into said dungeons. Each player creates their own version of a challenging dungeon filled with traps, monsters, and treasures.

But you’re also forced to take on the dangers of your opponent’s crafted dungeon, to see who manages to come out on top. If you have fond memories of the hidden-info nature of old games like Battleship, but you want some greater strategic depth and fantasy flavor thrown in, this one is a great pick.

#4205. 10 Great Games That Defined The Original Xbox

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

25 years ago, on November 15th, 2001, the gaming industry was forever changed when Microsoft officially dived into the console gaming market with the debut of its first home console, simply called the Xbox.

Designed to be a bridge between the hardware and software capabilities of PCs and the accessibility of home gaming consoles, the original Xbox console took the world by storm with its revolutionary gaming titles and services, proving that the United States can still rival Japanese gaming prospects.

With the original Xbox, and the overall Xbox brand, celebrating its momentous 25th anniversary this November, here’s a look back at 10 great exclusive games that defined the original Xbox and helped pave the way for Microsoft to become a modern gaming juggernaut.

Today, Xbox is largely known for three exclusive franchises: Halo, Gears of War, and Forza but long before the latter simulation racing series took the Xbox brand by storm during the Xbox 360 era, there was another series that stood as Xbox’s premier exclusive racing franchise: Project Gotham Racing.

Originally released as one of the Xbox’s many launch titles, the first Project Gotham Racing allowed up to four players in split-screen multiplayer to race against each other using 29 of the hottest cars of the early 21st century across San Francisco, London, Tokyo, and New York City.

With its stunt-focused Kudos point system and fun, arcade-like modes, Project Gotham Racing became one of the earliest Platinum Hits on the Xbox, leading to the development of three direct sequels, a few spinoffs, and the hit Xbox Live Arcade game, Geometry Wars.

Every great console needs its own standout amusing party game, and while Nintendo had Mario Party and PlayStation had Crash Bash, Xbox got its own distinct party game in the form of Fuzion Frenzy.

Another Xbox launch title, Fuzion Frenzy was an original party game not based on any prior IP, with the game being set in a futuristic tournament pitting four players against one another across randomized or pre-selected minigames with the goal of obtaining as many orbs and points as possible.

Chaotic minigames like Paint Panic and Falling Star quickly made Fuzion Frenzy a fan-favorite, and while it only got one sequel on the Xbox 360, many players still go back to play its wacky games to this very day (thanks to FF being backwards compatible on every future Xbox platform).

The sixth generation of consoles was a time for beginnings and a time for endings for many in the gaming industry at the time, most notably Sega. The Sega Dreamcast would mark the end for its home console prospects.

However, the failure of the Dreamcast didn’t mark the end for several Sega properties, as Microsoft collaborated with Sega to make the Xbox the exclusive home for several Dreamcast ports and sequels. Arguably the best was the funky Jet Set Radio Future.

A sequel to Jet Grind Radio, Jet Set Radio Future is a hyper stylized action game set in a futuristic Tokyo, where a group of teenagers called the GGs skate throughout the city and spray paint graffiti as a form of resistance against the dominating Rokkaku Group megacorporation.

Fans of the original Xbox who want play adventure titles that feature villains as protagonists should check out these 10 games

The RPG giant that is Bethesda is currently owned by Microsoft, and is a major part of Xbox’s future game investments. The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel is rumored to become a Project Helix exclusive, but long before Microsoft purchased Bethesda, the two companies first collaborated to release The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind exclusively on the original Xbox.

The first Elder Scrolls title to debut on a home console, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind was a first and third-person RPG set in the titular ash-clouded Tamriel province of Morrowind, following a customizable prisoner who sets out on a journey to defeat the oppressive Dagoth Ur.

While Morrowind hasn’t aged as well as its successors, it paved the way for Bethesda to debut other landmark RPGs, such as Fallout, Skyrim, and Starfield on consoles, helping showcase the immense potential of western RPGs.

One of the greatest innovations the original Xbox featured was the creation of Xbox Live, as it was one of the first online multiplayer gaming services designed for home consoles and practically laid the groundwork for all modern online gaming services. Xbox Live’s debut title was MechAssault.

Set in the multimedia BattleTech franchise, MechAssault is a third-person mech shooter game set on the planet Helios. It follows a Wolf's Dragoons BattleMech pilot as they attempt to liberate the planet from the technology-worshipping faction Word of Blake.

MechAssault’s campaign is a lot of fun, but the game is far more famous for its multiplayer as it was one of the first console titles to feature Quick Matches, the ability to host and invite friends to online games, and multiplayer DLC such as new maps, gametypes, and new types of mechs like Raven and Loki.

Every sixth generation console featured fantastic titles that were beloved by many but just didn’t sell well enough to receive proper sequels, resulting in these types of games becoming cult classics. There’s no better Xbox cult classic out there than Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge.

Loosely based on the 1998 Crimson Skies board game, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge has players embody Fortune Hunters air pirate gang leader Nathan Zachary, in an alternate 20th century where planes and zeppelins became the primary mode of transportation and the U.S. split into warring nations.

With an interesting world and story highly reminiscent of classic pulp books and films like Indiana Jones and enthralling third-person fighter plane gameplay, Revenge quickly became a fan-favorite. While it never received a sequel, it has since become the unofficial mascot for Xbox’s backwards compatibility.

These classic games will require some work to play again unless you have an older-gen console.

Early on in the Xbox brand’s history, Xbox’s most famous exclusive franchises were Halo, Gears of War, and Peter Molyneux's highly ambitious fantasy RPG Fable, which is finally set to return to Xbox early next year with a reboot of the series.

The original Fable was claimed by Molyneux to be the most ambitious RPG of the sixth console generation, with the game supposedly allowing players to have children in-game, play through the protagonist’s entire life, and witness plant life grow throughout the game, among other promises.

While most of these features weren’t present in the first Fable game, the original Fable still turned out to be an incredibly charming, comedic, and overall fun RPG, thanks to its witty British humor, morality system, and vast numbers of ways to interact with NPCs such as getting married and farting on people.

Nintendo fans recently got to take part in the midnight launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launch at various gaming stores. Those launch events paled in comparison to the cultural phenomenon that was the launch of Halo 2.

The original Xbox was arguably the house Halo: Combat Evolved built, and as such, most gamers in the world were excited to see how Bungie would improve upon the series in Halo 2, leading to the sequel receiving 1.5 million U.S. pre-orders and selling over 2.4 million copies in its launch day alone.

This anticipation was warranted though, as Halo 2 became the most popular Xbox Live game up until the release of Gears of War 1 and is widely regarded to feature one of the best FPS campaigns of all time thanks to the introduction of the Arbiter, dual-wielding, vehicle hijacking, and more.

The original Xbox was home to very few JRPGs, but these obscure ones might have something left exploring if you're interested.

While Fable 1 is the RPG most associated with the original Xbox, I would argue that it wasn’t the best RPG available on the console, with that honor instead going to BioWare’s epic 2003 masterpiece Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

Many Star Wars video games were released exclusively for the original Xbox, but KOTOR was by far the most notable. It not only took place roughly 4,000 years before the events of the films during the Jedi Civil War, but featured one of the greatest gaming twists of all time, centered around Darth Revan.

KOTOR’s rather clunky round-based combat hasn't exactly aged well over the years, but its story and characters are still regarded as being some of the best to appear any RPG, such as Darth Malak, Jedi Knight Bastila Shan, the murderous droid HK-47, and the Mandalorian Canderous Ordo to name a few.

Finally, without a doubt, the number one exclusive video game that defined the original Xbox and arguably the Xbox brand overall was the launch title and Bungie’s revolutionary FPS Halo: Combat Evolved.

Halo: Combat Evolved was the definitive console-based FPS that truly showcased the capability of consoles to deliver an engaging, fun, and wondrous FPS experience, thanks to its cinematic quality, wide-open spaces, addictive gunplay and vehicle combat, and engrossing FPS multiplayer maps.

If Halo: Combat Evolved hadn’t been packaged with most Xbox consoles on day one, Xbox likely wouldn’t have lasted beyond the sixth generation of consoles and CE’s success ultimately led to Xbox not only obtaining a mascot with Master Chief but the creation of one of the most beloved sci-fi multimedia franchises of all time.

#4201. Interview: Goddess of Victory Nikke's dev team tell all about the hit shooter for its 4th anniversary

With Goddess of Victory: Nikke's fourth anniversary event just having taken place, the hit character-collecting shooter is riding high on its enduring popularity. This got us a bit curious about how things work behind the scenes with the folks at Shift Up.

So, we got the chance not only to put our questions to the dev team as a whole, but also to some specific members, such as graphics group lead Park Sanghu! Read on to find out more about what they had to say about this massive milestone year for Goddess of Victory: Nikke. General Dev Team Over the past four years, what have been the most exciting moments for Goddess of Victory: Nikke?

With NIKKE, we've always hoped to create events where mini-games, the 3D field, the story, the music, and the characters all come together and bring out the best in each other.

From that point of view, OVER ZONE was probably the most thrilling moment for us. It was the first time our vision for an event landed the way we hoped it would.

Honestly, if we could pick more than one, we would say every single anniversary event, because every anniversary and half-anniversary event has been a challenge for us, and each time the response from our Commanders has been gratifying.

We think there are so many games out there in the world, each offering something different to enjoy. NIKKE has a lot to offer too, but we would say the story has played the biggest part in its success.

We think a game's appeal depends on the timing being right. Fortunately, it seems the kind of experience we wanted to offer reached players at just the right time. In that sense, we've been genuinely lucky, and we're always grateful to our Commanders for the love they show to NIKKE.

Our design priorities vary depending on the Nikke's affiliation. For a manufacturer-affiliated Nikke, what matters is a design where the character's personality and concept come through at a glance—something that catches your interest and makes it easy to see the character's appeal.

Pilgrims, on the other hand, need to feel distinct from regular Nikkes. We want anyone who sees them to be left with a striking, flamboyant impression, so we focus on Nikke's signature original details and a high level of design intricacy, which give it a distinctive look.

Just as we previewed in the Developer's Note, and as demonstrated by some of the content showcased during the 4th Anniversary, we plan to continue building out features and systems that let players get even deeper into the story. We will share a more detailed roadmap in a future Developer's Note, so please stay tuned.

First of all, we are thrilled that we are now able to support Spanish in the game. Because we dedicate so much passion and effort to our story, We hope that Spanish language support brings enjoyment to even more of our Commanders.

Our hope is that even more fans will be able to enjoy wonderful experiences with NIKKE through offline events and expanded text language options in the future.We will do everything we can to help make that a reality. Park Sanghu (Graphics Group Lead) What makes Nikke's graphical style so distinct?

We would say Nikke's distinctive art style comes from the balance between three things: subtle rendering that brings out the full appeal of each character, a very high density of detail, and bold staging that ties it all together.

In particular, it's important to us to bring out each character's unique personality and silhouette while giving the same care to the finer details, from costumes and equipment to the texture of each material.

On top of that, we use lighting, colour, and composition to show each character at their best. We think that combination is what makes Nikke's art style so distinctive.

Our design priorities vary depending on the Nikke's affiliation. For a manufacturer-affiliated Nikke, what matters is a design where the character's personality and concept come through at a glance—something that catches your interest and makes it easy to see the character's appeal.

Pilgrims, on the other hand, need to feel distinct from regular Nikkes. We want anyone who sees them to be left with a striking, flamboyant impression, so we focus on Nikke's signature original details and a high level of design intricacy, which give it a distinctive look. Ju Jonghyeon a.k.a. Cosmograph (Sound Director) How did you approach the soundscape of Nikke? Stuff like the music, SFX and whatnot?

We believe that sound in games is more of a feedback element. That's why we always keep in mind what the top priority should be in each situation when working on the sound.

For interactions such as Character Touch SFX, our top priority is to bring out each character's charm. For Maria-n in the 4th Anniversary update, we wanted to further emphasise the musical contrast between different situations. We created a clear distinction between the music before and after meeting the Commander. By reducing the overall musical density, we aimed to bring each text-based action to life through sound.

We're always grateful to everyone who has continued to trust us and wait patiently.We will do our utmost to deliver a better game and an improved service.

Now that what could be considered Part 1 of the story has largely unfolded, we believe we can offer players a fresher and more exciting experience in Part 2. Please continue to support us going forward, and we wish you all good health Some pretty interesting tidbits about what Nikke's development process is like, and a couple of hints about the future! While Nikke has had a rocky month with their recent PC launcher troubles, it seems that was only a bit of a stumble. So hopefully, in the future we'll see Goddess of Victory: Nikke once more going from strength to strength.

Of course, to do that they'll also have to cope with some other up-and-coming competitors. You can check out some of the biggest hits of the past year making waves on smartphones with our list of the best mobile games of 2026 (so far)!

#4199. Love and Deepspace ushers in the Year of the Horse with a Wuxia-inspired AU multi-banner and a restaurant management mini-game

A new Love and Deepspace banner event is here with a lot of rewards to earn, and brand-new Memories for all five lads to unlock.

Love and Deepspace has kicked off the next big in-game moment and is celebrating Chinese New Year with the arrival of a new 5-Star Memory Series. This year's spring-themed banner is available now until February 27, and it comes with a host of events.

The Mortality’s Tenderness banner features five new limited-time 5-Star Memories, one each for the game’s five love interests. The theme is all about warmth, reunion, and intimacy, taking place in a Wuxia-inspired setting that's once again an alternate universe from the main story of the game.

The new memory cards are Xavier: Blades with Blossoms, Zayne: Entwined Kites, Rafayel: Carved Gemheart, Sylus: Shared Lanterns, and Caleb: Clearday Return. You can pick three of the five to focus on and further pick one to guarantee on your second 5-star pull; and you can earn wish rewards by making cumulative wishes over the course of the event.

Some of the rewards you could get include limited headwear, Limited Deepspace Wishes, and — of course — Memory-themed outfits and hairstyles inspired by the new Memories. Outside of wish rewards, the Memory Series comes with growth tasks that rewards you with in-game materials for levelling up the new cards during the event. When you reach Rank 1 for any new Memory from the banner, you’ll earn a Memory-themed outfit with a special colour that matches your chosen love interest.

Illusio returns as part of the new event, too, letting you customise the look of Kindled Moments across all five new Memories. Things you can customise include selecting the outfits and accessories for each love interest, so you can recreate Kindled Moments in your own style. As always, Kindled Moments will go back to their default look after the event ends.

There’s a new mini-game to play, too, available only during the event. It’s called Courteous Fare, a frantic but familiar restaurant management simulation that allows you to unlock a variety of rewards.

Furthermore, if you log in for 10 days throughout the event, you can unlock a new outfit set, Wealth Overflow, which can be worn by any of the love interests as well as the heroine. There are other login rewards, too, like 10 Deepspace Wishes, 10 Empyrean Wishes, His and My Outfit sets, two dynamic portrait photo poses, and loads more.

Finally, the Golden Fortune event adds even more daily log in rewards in the form of one free "shake" per day, from which you can earn a random reward of between 68 and 108 Diamonds — that adds up to a total of 1,296 Diamonds if you show up every day.

#4198. Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”

“Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game."

While players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

My biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently announced Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

#4197. Warhammer Survivors review - "It's got the heart, but not the spark."

Back before Vampire Survivors hit iOS and Android, there were already a number of games inspired by (or, some might say, ripping off) their formula. So much so that I was wondering if it would go the way of Fall Guys/Stumble Guys, and be outshined by others who had gotten to mobile first.

But while those other games still have their fans, Poncle’s arrival on mobile only increased the popularity of Vampire Survivors. So much so that Auroch Digital reached out to create their own spinoff, dubbed Warhammer Survivors, that seeks to do for roguelites what Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun did for boomer shooters!

So, now Warhammer Survivors is out in the wild. But does it hold up to the indie hit that is Vampire Survivors? Hammer time If you’ve played Vampire Survivors, then you know what to expect from Warhammer Survivors. And to their credit, Auroch Digital maintain much of the same gameplay loop and fun of dealing with hordes of enemies, albeit with some interesting twists on the formula, such as different mechanics for each faction, like toxic debuffs from Nurgle or a hive-mind aspect for Tyranids.

For fans of AoS and 40,000, it's a robust offering, as Warhammer Survivors splits each universe into its own sub-game with its own progression. That means different levels, enemies and weapons, although many of them will feel somewhat similar in everything but looks.

If you’re a Vampire Survivors fan, this’ll all seem quite familiar, but Warhammer Survivors can also feel a lot more difficult due to the slower-paced movement of your character and the more dangerous enemies. Depending on your perspective, that’s either a good or a bad thing, but it definitely makes you feel as if there’s more at stake when you get cornered.

And while the weapons and gadgets feel familiar to what we've seen before, there are enough tweaks to make them feel different. One particularly interesting mechanic is that when you pick up a weapon your character is incompatible with, another character joins your party. While mostly cosmetic, their positioning affects where their attacks spring from, and if nothing else, it makes you feel as if you’re leading your own Kill Team into battle. Reference Overloaded Probably the most Warhammer thing about it is the number of references and nods to the original franchise. Whether that’s collecting paint pots to unlock new characters, all the iconic weapons, or even power-ups inspired by various gubbins from the hobby (blast templates, my beloved).

Basically, if you’ve ever been a fan of Warhammer 40,000 or Age of Sigmar, you’ll enjoy the nods to the hobby’s lengthy history. But if you’re a newcomer who, for whatever reason, has picked this up as your first Warhammer experience, you’ll be left feeling somewhat confused.

Imperium Sound (& Graphics) System One aspect where Warhammer Survivors is thrashed by the original Vampire Survivors is in its soundtrack and SFX. The bit-crushed music and impact of weapons don’t match up to the original, and feel more than a little flat at times. I was excited to hear about the 80s/90s rock and electronic mashup music, but nothing really hits the same way that tracks such as Mad Forest, Moms are Tough, or Gatti Amari do when you’re really in the zone.

The graphics, however, are perfectly acceptable, albeit without the same amount of charm as Vampire Survivors. But you’ll find all your favourite Warhammer characters crushed up into some tasty bits that make them instantly recognisable, but also feel distinctly Survivors-like, and the colourful locations manage to feel authentically grimdark while contrasting one another.

Oi- we’re the bloody Ubersreik five! Now, there is one big omission here, and, of course, it’s the setting of The Old World. Not to sound like a grognard, but while Age of Sigmar is a perfectly worthy setting to draw from, Warhammer Fantasy, which kicked off the entire IP, has roared back into popularity in recent years. We get Gotrek Gurnisson, undoubtedly one of the most recognisable characters from The Old World, but no other nods to the original grimdark fantasy universe.

It’s a shame, because what’s already here is a great love letter to Warhammer. Hopefully, we’ll see some updates down the line, and heck, I’d even take a paid DLC to see content inspired by Warhammer Fantasy make an appearance. With more updates down the line, this could be the case, and there’re plenty of spinoffs in Games Workshop’s wider line that’d make for excellent one-off levels or characters to join the battle. So here’s hoping Auroch take advantage of the vast depth of the IP. Grindhammer I actually put off publishing this review because I wanted to put more time into Warhammer Survivors. And I did, to the tune of around three or so hours, which isn’t much in the grand scheme of things but usually more than enough to get a feel for a game; especially a fast-paced roguelite. Yet, I couldn’t help but feel I was missing something that might really change how I felt about it. But every time I played, it felt like I was making only the most incremental progress, even though (as you'll find) I was chugging along at a quite even pace.

And to me, that’s my main issue with Warhammer Survivors. Whereas Vampire Survivors feels like it moves fast, with you quickly unlocking new stages, weapons and abilities, Warhammer Survivors is much slower in terms of progression. Add to that the fact that you have two separate universes with (mostly) completely different progression, and what should be exciting, rapid progress quickly becomes a slog.

Although it’s been a while, I feel as if in five hours of Vampire Survivors I was already headed towards that 30-minute mark, exploring multiple levels and already well on my way to experiencing new weapon fusions and upgrades. Maybe it’s me getting older, or it’s that Warhammer Survivors simply feels smaller and less engaging than its spiritual predecessor, especially considering that even though I felt I was making slow progress, it seems I've already completed 14% of the 40k side of the equation!

A lot of the issues with progression and how slow it seems, I feel, are that aforementioned difficulty. Now, there’s a joke about game journalists and difficulty there, but let me explain. In Vampire Survivors, you’re encouraged to move, to explore the map and dodge enemies, thereby encountering more secrets and upgrades. Meanwhile, Warhammer Survivors’ more punishing damage encourages you to hunker down, and only move if you see an existing secret highlighted on the map.

That means that, while you play for the same amount of time, you feel as if you’ve found less (even if you've actually found more). And yes, it’s perfectly fun watching hordes of Tyranids fall to your bolters and las-rifle fire, but it’s not quite as exciting as whipping your way through hordes of bats. While it may be more Warhammer to pick a spot and stick to it as you fortify your position, it sort of misses the point of a fast-paced bullet heaven.

Point being, I love Warhammer, I love Vampire Survivors; so this should have me in a chokehold. But it simply doesn’t. It feels like a perfectly fine love letter to the franchise, yet it never quite hits the heights that Vampire Survivors did. And while it may feel unfair for me to continuously compare the two, it’s hard not to when Survivors is in the title.

Maybe, with the coming updates Auroch have promised, it’ll be able to stand on its own two feet. Even so, I can heartily recommend it if you’re either a Warhammer fan, or you’ve completely rinsed everything Vampire Survivors has to offer. Just be aware that recommendation comes with a few asterisks.

#4195. Battlefield 6's next season will speed up battle pass progression, and make it so Redsec players who don't own the game can actually make progress

Season 2 of Battlefield 6 looks to bring a host of broad, positive changes to XP, progression, audio and more.

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

The real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the new season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

#4194. Grand Theft Auto VI Will Run At 30 FPS On All Consoles, But PS5 Pro Will Feature 'Improved Clarity' And Ray-Traced Shadows

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on Thursday, November 19, and you can preload the game on your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S starting today, Rockstar Games has announced. The studio has also revealed what kind of visuals players can expect on their respective consoles, making clear that regardless of where you play, GTA VI targets 30 FPS gameplay.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life – while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants," Rockstar writes in a blog post.

Rockstar Games also breaks down the different graphical settings available on PlayStation and Xbox consoles. On PS5 Pro, GTA VI will feature "improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro." On PS5 and PS5 Pro, the game will include "high-fidelity haptic feedback" fully integrated into DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D audio, and improved load times, "making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles."

On Xbox consoles, Rockstar doesn't dive into performance; instead, it focuses on Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox Series X/S and Xbox One consoles, noting this feature will use Xbox Series S graphics settings.

GTA VI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

For more, check out the song "Pusher" from the game's original score, then check out the GTA VI launch trailer. After that, check out this exclusive story about how GTA VI features over 170 animal species and another about its tropical storms and hurricanes.
